content:
Episode 7 Grades 3-12: Grow & Grade with Rubrics — Introduction and Rubric Overview

Hi, I'm KS, and thanks for joining me for the TEACH Writing PD Mini-Series. In this video, we'll explore how to adapt a kid-friendly writing rubric that is easy for students to understand, aligns with state expectations, and works across various writing units. The examples and strategies shared here target paragraph-level writing. However, if you work with Level 1 or 2 English language learners, students with special needs, or those who communicate primarily through pictures and words, you might find the Primary version of this video to be more relevant to your needs.

Scoring writing can be a sensitive topic. Many teachers feel unsure when grading writing. While others find the process arbitrary, subjective, or based on personal opinion. While these concerns are valid, they can be alleviated by using an analytic, instructional rubric. Let's quickly review the key points from Episode 4, where this concept was first introduced.

A rubric, of course, is an assessment tool used to determine the quality of a student's writing. Analytic means the writing will earn separate scores for the different traits or components, highlighting individual strengths and weaknesses. An analytic rubric provides a more precise evaluation, identifying areas of excellence and those needing improvement — this indicates to a student what to revise in this piece or in future writings. An instructional rubric includes only the skills that have been explicitly taught, modeled, and practiced. This distinction matters when considering the rubrics used on state tests or end-course assessments — these reflect year-end grade-level expectations. Consequently, using those rubrics throughout the year may unfairly assess skills students haven't yet learned.

Episode 7 Grades 3-12: Grow & Grade with Rubrics — Growing Rubric Concept

In Episode 4 I outlined the facets of a rubric and decisions you would need to make. This included deciding the format and medium that you would display the rubric within, the range of levels you would include, and the traits or categories that you would assess. Within Episode 4, I also explained the process for building an initial classroom-based instructional rubric, emphasizing the importance of involving students in the process. Early in the year, this typically results in a simple, sparse rubric, as students will only include writing skills they are already familiar with.

However, as the term "initial" suggests, this first rubric captures only the early stages of learning and quickly becomes outdated. Instructional writing rubrics are meant to evolve, expanding as you introduce, teach, model, and practice new skills. As your teaching progresses, so should your rubric. One key advantage of an instructional rubric is that it keeps previously taught skills relevant. Many students tend to isolate or silo writing skills, assuming earlier lessons no longer apply once a new unit begins. But a growing rubric includes the foundational criteria while incorporating new skills after they have been taught and practiced. Importantly, an instructional rubric doesn't change its expectations — it grows them. It doesn't shift its focus but broadens the range of skills it assesses. This cumulative approach holds students accountable for increasingly rigorous standards, aligning expectations with what they've been taught. Instructional rubrics follow the mantra — Teach more. Expect more.

Episode 7 Grades 3-12: Grow & Grade with Rubrics — Instructional vs. State Rubrics

To clarify, this is different from the year-long rubrics often used on standardized tests or end-of-course assessments. These rubrics are static and do not change; they outline grade-level writing expectations for the end of the year. While they are essential for tracking data, they are not ideal for classroom use because they assess skills that students haven't yet learned. That's where the instructional rubric is so important. With its growing criteria, it helps students focus on what they should prioritize without overwhelming them or assessing skills they haven't been taught yet.

Although state or end-of-course rubrics are not used by students on a daily basis, they should be referenced frequently by the teacher. As you expand the class instructional rubric, include similar skills and expectations as they are taught. In other words, your rubric should evolve to prepare students for state test success. With this long-term goal in mind, it's not necessary for individual classroom rubrics to be identical throughout the year — what matters is that they all evolve toward the same endpoint by "Game Day."

section_name: When and Where to Update the Rubric
content:
Episode 7 Grades 3-12: Grow & Grade with Rubrics — When and Where to Update the Rubric

With a clearer understanding of why growing an instructional writing rubric is powerful, let's shift to the logistics of when, where, and how to update it.

WHEN do you update the rubric? With the initial rubric sufficing for a short while, don't rush to add new criteria to the rubric immediately after introducing each new skill. Provide students time to practice the writing skill before they are held accountable for it. Consider updating the rubric about once a month, after 3-5 new skills have been introduced and practiced, or as you wrap up a unit. While the rubric isn't updated daily or weekly, it's also not something that stays the same all year. For those concerned about time, consider this: updating the rubric with students takes roughly the same amount of time as passing out and explaining a rubric that you created. We're not necessarily adding extra time; instead, we're repurposing the time in a way that involves students more directly. In fact, having students participate in the process provides them with an additional opportunity to engage with the skills you'll be assessing.

WHERE do you add the new criteria? When adding a new skill to your rubric, you won't simply tack it onto the bottom of the list. Instead, integrate it within the broader trait or category it represents. This approach helps students understand how individual skills connect to larger writing competencies and how they contribute to their individual scores. If you've made a physical rubric, you'll need to make space for new criteria within each row. This might involve cutting, taping, and adding paper to your classroom display. By maintaining the same color-coding and grouping similar skills, you help students visually connect individual skills to their writing traits. A digital template makes it easy to update your rubric quickly and efficiently. You can insert new criteria within the appropriate trait rows, make any necessary adjustments, and share the updated version with both students and parents with just a few clicks.

section_name: How to Update Rubric Criteria with Students
content:
Episode 7 Grades 3-12: Grow & Grade with Rubrics — How to Update Rubric Criteria with Students

HOW do you update the rubric criteria? As I shared in Episode 4, it's vital to involve your students in the building of the class writing rubric — and again each time you update it. This ensures that their voice and understanding remain a key part of this assessment tool. The more students participate in developing the rubric, the better they understand its expectations and the more quickly they can integrate them within their own writing.

A rubric-updating lesson might begin like this: "Class, today we are going to update our rubric. We have learned and practiced several new skills but they aren't yet on our rubric. We've learned to include text evidence to support our ideas, transitions to link and connect ideas, and action verbs to strengthen the word choice and description. But again, these skills aren't represented anywhere within the rubric criteria. So, today we are going to quickly review what each of those skills means and update our rubric to include them."

After setting the lesson purpose, support students in thinking through their new understanding of each recently-taught skill. "Class, let's start with text evidence, which falls within the trait or category of Ideas. What did we learn about including text evidence in our writing?" Now, I'd expect kids to say "The writing has text evidence" or something like "it has good text evidence." And without any direction or support from the teacher, those are likely responses.

However, we know that rubric criteria describes how the skill looks and sounds in action — how it works and functions in writing. Therefore, ask guiding questions to remind students of the specifics they learned about this skill within your previous mini-lessons and their independent practice: "Class, what did I teach you about what counts as strong evidence? Where do you insert text evidence within writing? How do you integrate text evidence within a sentence or paragraph?"

Besides preparing students to update the rubric criteria, these questions serve as a quick formative assessment as to "what stuck" from your explicit teaching.

Episode 7 Grades 3-12: Grow & Grade with Rubrics — Parallel Criteria Across Rubric Levels

After spending a few minutes discussing their understanding of this newer skill, then capture their detailed description within a new bulleted criterion under the highest level. Encourage them to contribute verbiage to ensure the rubric reflects what they know and understand about this writing skill.

After describing the first skill at the highest level, guide students to consider what it looks and sounds like within each level below it. This is known as parallel criteria. If a skill is mentioned in one level, it needs to be mentioned in all of them. Each level of the rubric should describe the same ingredients — just at varying degrees of quality.

Likewise, that skill should be referenced across the rubric using the same academic language. If the high level refers to the "thesis statement," don't call it a "controlling idea" in another level. If one level uses the term "introduction," don't suddenly refer to it as a "hook" or "beginning" in another. Keeping the language consistent helps students recognize the same skills, regardless of where they fall on the rubric. Inconsistent terms can confuse students and make it harder for them to understand what they need to improve.

To create parallel criteria, guide students to adjust the smaller nuances of this skill. Here are five ways to achieve that: 1) Teach them how to adjust consistency or frequency — varying how often the skill is demonstrated. 2) They could modify adjectives — using terms that reflect progression. 3) Consider omitting or including small features of the skill as it is described across the levels. 4) Push for neutral language, encouraging terms that describe performance without negative connotations. 5) Or provide parallel examples to depict what each level looks and sounds like.

Follow these parameters to flesh out parallel criteria for each of the recently-taught skills. In our class example, I would expand the rubric to include criteria for text evidence, transition phrases, and action verbs. If you teach multiple sections, repeat the process with all of your classes, presenting a merged version of the updated instructional rubric the next day.

section_name: Applying One Rubric Across Writing Units and Modes
content:
Episode 7 Grades 3-12: Grow & Grade with Rubrics — Applying One Rubric Across Writing Units and Modes

Let me pause for a moment to highlight another advantage of developing rubrics with your students. For teachers who may feel unsure about scoring writing, this collaborative process will not only help craft the new criteria, but it will expand and deepen your own understanding of the skills. Remember, you're not creating the rubric alone; you're growing it alongside your students.

Let's examine how this rubric can be applied to different units. While many educators believe each genre requires a distinct rubric, developing separate ones for every type of writing can be tedious and repetitive. Instead, let's look at how a single, evolving rubric can be tailored to fit various units throughout the year.

Although the rubric language is specific enough to differentiate levels, it's broad enough to apply to different modes. Therefore, it isn't necessary to create a separate rubric for each writing unit. If the rubric categories reflect the qualities of good writing, then they apply to a persuasive essay, informative report, or narrative story. While some teachers prefer to build a new rubric for each unit, it's worth considering how the same growing instructional rubric could be used to fit all the units. To make this work, we need to show students how to tweak the interpretation of the rubric criteria to fit the purpose of the next assignment.

For example, if one of the criteria states that "Ideas are well developed with supporting details," then: In a narrative, this means that there is an identifiable problem with a clear and reasonable solution. In an informative, this means that there are relevant facts and specifics per main idea. In an argumentative, this means that there are clear reasons with specific evidence/examples for each.

If the criterion stated that "Ideas are organized logically," then this would vary in its interpretation: In a narrative, this means that the plot moves chronologically. In an informative, this means that similar info is grouped together. In an argumentative, this means that reasons are organized to maximize the impact.

If the criterion states that "Quotations added interest," then this could also vary in its interpretation: In a narrative, this means that character dialogue is interesting and relevant. In an informative, this means that expert quotes are interesting and relevant. In an argumentative, this means that testimonials are interesting and relevant.

Now, let me clarify that although most criteria is applicable across all writing, there are a few mode-specific skills. For example, a research paper assignment might assess that information is used from three or more sources, and that those sources are identified within a Works Cited Page. Well, I definitely want to assess for those skills, so I will add them in a rubric-update lesson — but only temporarily. Then, when this unit is over, I could remove that criteria and resume using the same instructional rubric. By using one growing rubric, we create consistency and a clear focus across the year.

section_name: Scoring and Grading with the Rubric
content:
Episode 7 Grades 3-12: Grow & Grade with Rubrics — Scoring and Grading with the Rubric

We've spent most of our time discussing how to build, grow, and customize an instructional writing rubric you can use throughout the year. Now, let's turn our attention to scoring and grading with that tool. Using AI, teachers can input rubric criteria to efficiently, consistently, and instantly score student writing. However, it's crucial to balance this with times when we, the teacher, review student writing ourselves. AI apps often struggle to appreciate the nuances of writing, apps may be limited in their understanding of some content, and most can't comment on unique writer strengths or weaknesses.

That said, human scoring also has limitations — beyond the obvious time commitment. One challenge of the human brain is its difficulty in recalibrating quickly between very high and very low writing samples. To avoid inconsistent scoring, stay anchored to the rubric and organize the samples before grading. Quickly skim and sort the class writing into high, middle, and low piles — or, if reading digital writing, determine your virtual piles. Then, score half of the middle-level writing, followed by all of the lower-level samples. Then, score the remaining middle-level writings, before finishing with the high-level pieces. This approach prevents large jumps between differing quality levels, helping to achieve consistent, objective scoring.

Throughout the process, regularly reference the rubric and focus solely on the listed criteria. Avoid memorizing the rubric! Frequent checks help prevent drifting from the stated expectations. The rubric isn't just a scoring tool — it ensures consistency and minimizes personal biases.

Episode 7 Grades 3-12: Grow & Grade with Rubrics — Rubric Feedback and Calculating Grades

In fact, you could force yourself to reference the rubric regularly by using it as a tool to communicate feedback. Instead of writing comments like "Add more detail" on a student's paper, highlight the relevant criteria on the rubric and cite the paragraph number it pertains to. This approach is especially helpful to explain a Level 2 score, as students will see criteria highlighted from both Levels 1 and 3. Likewise, instead of marking every grammar and mechanical error in a student's writing, focus on highlighting recurring weaknesses on the rubric. After scoring the writings, return each student's piece with an annotated rubric. This not only prompts students to reflect and revise but also holds them accountable for the criteria they helped create.

Calculating grades: With the traits or categories scored on the analytic rubric, many teachers make the mistake of adding up the levels to determine a student's grade. But that presumes that levels are points — and that is incorrect.

Let's first establish 3 guiding principles when it comes to calculating grades from an analytic rubric. Guiding Principle 1: The lowest rubric level is not failure. It represents weak writing, but it's still part of the grading system. Weak writing is different from not submitting an assignment — which earns a zero. Guiding Principle 2: Use the highest rubric level to acknowledge those who exceed expectations. This motivates students to strive for excellence and rewards exemplary work. Guiding Principle 3: Not all traits are equal. Different rubric categories matter more depending on the assignment. For instance, in a first draft — ideas and organization should weigh more than conventions, while in a poetry assignment, word choice or style may be valued higher.

Honoring these three guiding principles, we avoid simply adding up rubric levels. This is why I prefer naming the levels with a baseball theme — single, double, triple, home run, grand slam. Using names instead of numbers eliminates the temptation to add scores and encourages both students and teachers to focus on a clear process.

section_name: Converting Rubric Scores to Grades and Closing
content:
Episode 7 Grades 3-12: Grow & Grade with Rubrics — Converting Rubric Scores to Grades and Closing

Here is how to convert rubric scores to grades or points: Step 1: Select the Traits to Assess — Focus on the most relevant categories for the assignment rather than scoring every row on the rubric. Be sure to communicate these traits to students before they begin writing. Step 2: Allocate Assignment Points — Decide the total point value of the assignment and distribute points across the selected traits based on their importance. For example, in a 50-point first-draft assignment, you might assign 25 points to ideas, 15 to organization, and 10 to conventions. Step 3: Calculate Point Values per Cell — Determine the percentage of the total points for each level in the rubric row. Now, after scoring the writing using the criteria on the analytic instructional rubric, calculate the points per cell to generate the student's grade.

Many teachers use a rubric calculator to simplify this process, as it automatically converts trait levels into points. This allows teachers to focus on analyzing students' strengths and weaknesses in writing while the calculator handles the math. For more details on how to use the rubric calculator, check out the hyperlink in the digital handout from Episode 7.

As I wrap up this video, let me identify the most important takeaways. Analytic instructional writing rubrics: 1) Are made with students. 2) Start simple and grow with instruction. 3) Can evolve to align with end-year assessment goals. By empowering students with an assessment tool that they understand, we take the next step toward building better writers.
